segments.speaker: John
segments.text: In a graduate course on Robot Learning and Contact-Rich Manipulation, today's lecture is on Blind Precise Assembly: Proprioceptive Sim-to-Real Peg-in-Hole for Diverse Parts. Work such as AlphaNIST and InsertionWM reflects a field exploring shared assembly policies and visual world models. This paper, from an M-I-T team, asks whether a robot can instead use changes in its own joint motion to guide precise contact. That matters when tight fits are hard to see or model. Yes, Noah?

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: Hi Professor, does blind here mean the robot has no sensors at all?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: No. Blind means the acting policy receives no images, force or torque readings, tactile input, hole pose, or part model. It does receive encoder-derived information about its own joints and gripper. The practical example is a peg that must enter a close-fitting hole: the policy begins with the peg already touching the fixture near the opening, then searches locally. The paper demonstrates this task on hardware; gear meshing and nut threading are simulated demonstrations.

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: The central idea is to treat proprioception—the robot’s own joint positions and velocities—as an indirect contact signal. When a peg touches the hole’s rim, the arm’s motion differs from what its commands would produce without contact. The policy reads a 0.6-second history of joint positions and velocities, along with gripper motion and prior actions, then adjusts its joint targets. In effect, it uses the mismatch between intended and observed motion to decide where to search next.

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: Quick question: how does the policy learn what those motion changes mean?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: Training supplies extra guidance, but not to the deployed actor. A decoder predicts simulated contact states from the history representation, helping train the encoder; the decoder is removed for deployment. The training critic also gets privileged simulator information, while the actor does not. The arm learns three simulated tasks: peg insertion, gear meshing, and nut threading. This setup encourages the policy’s history to retain information about contact, without giving the acting policy a direct contact label.

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: The authors test whether the policy’s history matters, rather than simply assuming it does. A probe can predict task modes from the history representation more accurately than from the current observation alone: 61 to 73% versus 41 to 64%, with 14% chance performance. In a latent-swap test, replacing a state’s history representation with one from another mode changes the action more than a same-mode swap. That supports mode-relevant history, but does not prove the representation is entirely about contact.

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: Can you clarify what the latent-swap result tells us, and what it cannot establish?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: It shows that the policy’s action depends on historical information in a way that varies with the task mode. For example, a searching state paired with an engaged-mode latent tends to produce a larger action change than a swap between two searching states. Across the reported tasks, some different-mode swaps change actions 1.3 to 3 times as much as same-mode swaps. This is evidence for history-dependent behavior, not proof that contact alone caused the action or explains every part of the latent.

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: A useful comparison separates movement distance from speed. In simulation, the blind peg policy travels a median 37 millimeters laterally before seating, versus 95 millimeters for a scripted spiral. But that spiral is an unusually favorable baseline: it starts flush with the opening and gets the peg orientation and best search direction. The blind policy is slower than the visual policy in the tested task, with median seating times of 0.80 seconds versus 0.44 seconds.

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: So does the blind policy generalize better because it searches through contact rather than matching visual features?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: That is the authors’ interpretation, not a uniquely established cause. Their matched simulation comparison holds task, resets, randomization, rewards, actions, and success checks constant, while comparing proprioceptive and wrist-camera policies. Both work well on training-like pegs. On held-out random convex pegs, however, the blind policy succeeds in 36.2% of episodes, compared with 3.9% for vision. The blind policy still fails in most of those episodes, so this is an advantage on that test, not universal robustness.

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: Keep that simulation result separate from the hardware evaluation: the deployed peg policy was trained on a broader mix of polygonal, smooth, and mixed cross-sections. With its parameters unchanged, it seats pegs in 173 of 237 real trials, or 73%, on a Flexiv Rizon 4S arm. It also succeeds on three held-out pegs with tighter clearance, a larger cross-section, and a taller handle. The hardware demonstration concerns peg insertion only, not the simulated gear and nut policies.

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: How should we relate this to visual assembly work such as InsertionWM?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: InsertionWM uses a visual world model alongside proprioception, while this paper tests whether joint-history feedback alone can guide local contact search. These approaches address different sensing and modeling choices, so the results do not establish that vision is generally inadequate. The paper’s matched simulation study does show a specific tradeoff: vision is faster on in-distribution peg insertion, while the blind policy handles some unseen shapes more reliably. The comparison gives evidence about these tested policies, not every possible visual or contact-based design.

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: The broader implication is that joint encoders may offer useful contact information without adding a force sensor, especially when the task starts near the place where contact must be resolved. But the boundary is important: this is a last-mile skill, not a search from anywhere. Trials begin with the peg touching the fixture near the hole, and the policy searches locally; it does not recover a peg that slips from the gripper and lands far away.

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: What would be the next useful test of this approach?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: A natural next step is to test how far contact-guided policies can expand their starting conditions and recover from larger disturbances, while keeping sensing and training assumptions explicit. Researchers could also compare richer visual and proprioceptive combinations under matched protocols. For now, the paper’s contribution is narrower and clearer: a history of the robot’s own motion can support precise, contact-started peg insertion, transfer to real hardware, and improve performance on particular unseen geometries in simulation.

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: The memorable takeaway is that a robot can learn to feel a fit through its joints: contact changes motion, and motion history can guide the next adjustment. That does not make the skill universal, nor does it eliminate vision’s strengths. It shows that for a local assembly problem, proprioception can carry enough information to search and seat a peg, including on hardware without fine-tuning. Thanks for listening.
